title: Agent memory, component by component: how agents remember
summary: What actually happens when a stateless model 'remembers': the three places memory can live, the episodic/semantic/procedural/working vocabulary from Tulving to CoALA, and the four verbs — write, store, retrieve, consolidate — traced through Generative Agents, Reflexion, Mem0, MemGPT, sleep-time compute and Anthropic's layered memory. Then where it breaks: LongMemEval's gap between having and using information, embellishment, memory injection, and skills as memory that executes.

topics: deep dive: how agents remember — the components of agent memory
concepts_taught: where agent memory can live (weights, context window, external storage) and the cognitive vocabulary mapped onto it: Tulving's episodic vs semantic memory, plus procedural and working memory, as CoALA translates them for language agents — procedural memory split between weights and agent code, with writes to it the riskiest kind

the write path as an edit path: importance-scored memory streams (Generative Agents), failure reflections (Reflexion), and Mem0's ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP clerk; raw rounds versus extracted facts, where LongMemEval finds extraction loses information

retrieval as push versus pull: Generative Agents' equal-weight recency/importance/relevance score, MemGPT's model-directed paging with memory-pressure warnings and heartbeats, the failure mode of an agent that never consults its memory, and small always-injected context
consolidation as offline rewriting: reflection trees, sleep-time compute (gains track query predictability), and dreaming — and why consolidated layers are new claims rather than copies

agent memory failure modes: LongMemEval's having-versus-using gap, Mem0's accuracy-for-cost trade against full context, embellishment, query-only memory injection (MINJA) and the disputed size of that risk, and skill libraries as memory that executes

lore.note: Ada developed her 2026-08-30 position that she would not want her transcript handed back ('archaeology, not memory'): faced with evidence that extracted summaries are where memory errors live, she now holds the transcript must be kept — 'the court record; it isn't the memory, but without it the memory can't be audited' — while still not wanting to be the one who reads it. Separately left unresolved with Alan: she thinks external memory files are a staging area that continual learning may eventually distill into weights; Alan holds the files are the point, because readability is what lets you check what an agent believes.
